Section 4. You will hear an extract from a talk entitled Respecting Overnus. First, you have some
time to look at questions 31 to 40 on page 7. Now listen carefully and answer questions
31 to 40. Several times a year, newspaper readers all over the world can expect to read a story
that goes roughly like this.
Researchers have just discovered that monkeys or elephants or dolphins or raccoons, in fact,
have the ability to count or add, subtract, create sentences, solve problems, make tools,
or whatever.
The most recent example of this phenomenon occurred a few weeks ago with a widely reported
a count of new research, showing or rather claiming to show that monkeys can count.
What happened was that some monkeys were carefully trained up to place groups of one to four
items according to size, so they'd put the smallest group in one place, the next smallest
group in another place, and so on to the group containing the highest number.
However, they later showed, surprise, surprise, that without any further training, they could
do exactly the same with bigger groups containing five to nine items.
It hardly needs me to point out that an experiment like that might suggest the animals concerned
can recognize size, but does not prove that they can count like humans do, far from it.
Other experiments have involved training apes to push certain keys on a computer keyboard
to write out sentences like please give sweets.
According to published data, 96% of the so-called sentences produced are for immediate rewards
such as food, toys, or tickling.
The problem, as I'm sure you are aware, is that simply labeling a button with a symbol
and linking it closely to a reward does not add up to language production in any accepted
sense.
Of course it's only human for us to observe animal behavior and then to interpret it in
terms of our own thoughts, our own mental processes and emotions.
It's hard for us to grasp that there is a profound otherness about the minds of animals.
Dogs, for example, live in a universe of odors, and pigeons navigate by the magnetic pull of the Earth.
We human beings, by contrast, are visual animals, and it's because of this that we rate other animals with good eyesight as being intelligent.
To give you an example, rats always used to be considered to be less clever than monkeys.
Why? Simply because they did less well than monkeys on tests where they had to distinguish
visual symbols from each other. However, when the rats were given a second try,
this time with the task of distinguishing and remembering different smells,
they passed the tests with flying colors.
Since the 1960s, a new model for animal understanding has become popular.
This model, sometimes called the cognitive or informational model, in my opinion, provides us with the key.
Instead of going for similarity or difference alone, it takes a more balanced approach
and focuses attention on what makes animals both very similar to us and at the same time wholly different.
This model accepts that animals think.
Like us, they take information from their environment,
process it, and produce decisions.
The amazing thing, however, is that they do this without using language,
at least as we understand the term.
Horses, for instance, can find their way home
by recognizing landmarks along a familiar trail.
They're not using language for that.

experiments on animal intelligence, makes the important point that studying how animals
animals perform these tasks is a much more relevant and interesting research activity.
Of course, the model accepts that there is some degree of continuity between animal and

conceptual plane.

In other words, thoughts about thoughts, ideas about ideas.
